a: Bildad the Shuhite
p: The second friend. 'Shuhite' probably ties him to Shuah, a son of Abraham and Keturah who lived in the east.
b: Bildad is introduced at 2:11. His title probably links him to Shuah, one of the sons Abraham had with Keturah and sent "to the land of the East" (Genesis 25:2; Genesis 25:6). Some scholars connect the name with Suhu, a land on the middle Euphrates known from Assyrian records, but that is uncertain. Like Eliphaz of Teman and Zophar of Naamah, Bildad is a wise man from outside Israel. The book sets its debate among the famous sages of the East (1 Kings 4:30), not in Jerusalem.

a: How long will your words be a mighty wind?
p: Bildad calls Job's speech wind: loud, strong, and empty. He answers Job's own words about wind in 6:26 and 7:7.
b: The Hebrew ruach kabbir is "a mighty wind." Wind in wisdom writing is the picture of talk with no weight (15:2; Ecclesiastes 1:14). Bildad picks up Job's own words: Job had said that his friends treat "a hopeless man's talk" as "only wind" (6:26) and that his life is wind (7:7). Bildad agrees with the first and turns it against him. The same word ruach can mean wind, breath or spirit, and Job will soon use it for the breath God will not let him catch (9:18).

a: Does God twist justice?
p: The verb means 'make crooked'. Bildad's whole speech rests on one point: God never bends what is right.
b: The verb 'ivvet means to bend or make crooked, as a dishonest merchant bends a scale (Amos 8:5) or a judge bends a case (Lamentations 3:36). Bildad sets justice (mishpat) and right (tsedeq) side by side, the two words Israel used for fair rule (Psalm 89:14). His question expects the answer no, and everything he says follows from it: if God cannot twist justice, Job's suffering must be deserved, or must be a test that will end well. Job does not deny God's power; he will use the same verb ('ivvetani) in 19:6: "it is God who has bent my case."
orig: הַאֵל יְעַוֵּת מִשְׁפָּט (ha'el ye'avvet mishpat), 'Does God make justice crooked?'

a: the Almighty
p: Shaddai, the old divine title used often in Job. 'Almighty' follows the Greek and Latin; its root meaning is debated.
b: Shaddai is one of the oldest titles of God, used in the stories of the ancestors (Genesis 17:1; Exodus 6:3) and 31 times in Job, more than in the rest of the Bible put together. The Greek often renders it pantokratōr, "ruler of all," and the Latin omnipotens, which gave English "the Almighty." Its origin is uncertain: proposals include "the one of the mountain" (from Akkadian shadu), "the one who is sufficient" (a rabbinic reading, she-dai), and a link with shad, "breast." The poet uses old names like Shaddai, El and Eloah to fit the book's setting before Moses. See the note on 12:9.

a: If your children sinned against him
p: Bildad says the children's death proves their sin. It is the friends' harshest line, and the reader knows it is wrong.
b: The reader knows from 1:5 that Job offered sacrifices in case his children had sinned, and from 1:12–19 that their death came from the test, not from a crime. Bildad does not know this. Read gently, "if" leaves room for hope: Job's children may have sinned and paid for it, but Job is alive, so he can still turn to God (8:5–7). Read harshly, it is a cruel syllogism: they died, so they sinned. Most commentators (Clines, Habel) hear both: Bildad means to offer Job a way out, but he does it by treating a father's grief as evidence.

a: the grip of their own rebellion
t: Into the hand of their rebellion
p: Literally 'he sent them into the hand of their rebellion': sin itself is the power that took them.
b: The Hebrew says God "sent them into the hand of their transgression." Sin is pictured as a master who takes custody of the sinner, as in Proverbs 5:22 (the wicked are caught in the cords of their own sin). Pesha' is rebellion, a breaking with a lord, not just a mistake. Bildad's picture is precise: God did not need to act; he only let their own rebellion take them. The Greek renders the line closely, "he sent them away by the hand of their lawlessness."
orig: בְּיַד־פִּשְׁעָם (beyad-pish'am), 'into the hand of their rebellion'

a: make your rightful home whole again
p: Literally 'restore the pasture-home of your righteousness': the home that a righteous man has a right to.
b: Shillam nevat tsidqekha is literally "he will make whole the dwelling of your righteousness." Naveh is a pasture or a herdsman's home, fitting a man whose wealth was flocks (1:3). The verb shillam (from the same root as shalom) means to make complete or to repay. Bildad promises that God will give back what Job's righteousness deserves, but the condition, "if you are pure and upright," quietly assumes that Job is not.

a: your later years will grow very large
p: Bildad's promise comes true in 42:12, but not for his reasons. The same pair of words, early and later, returns there.
b: Bildad's words reshit (beginning) and acharit (end, later life) come back in the epilogue: "the LORD blessed Job's later years more than his early ones" (42:12). The friend's prediction comes true, but only after God has said that the friends "did not say what is right about me" (42:7). Readers have long noticed the irony. Bildad was right about the ending and wrong about the reason: Job is restored not because he admitted guilt, but after he was told he spoke rightly.

a: Just ask the generation of long ago
p: Eliphaz appealed to a vision (4:12–21). Bildad appeals to the wisdom of past generations.
b: Each friend has a different source of certainty. Eliphaz told of a night vision (4:12–21). Bildad points to tradition: what the ancestors learned and handed down (compare Deuteronomy 32:7, "Ask your father, and he will tell you"). Zophar will appeal to God's hidden wisdom (11:6). Bildad's point is reasonable: one life is too short to learn the truth alone (8:9), so trust what many lives have tested. Job will answer that he knows the tradition as well as they do (12:3; 13:1–2), and that his own experience contradicts it.

a: We are yesterday
p: Bildad's short phrase: humans are newcomers, born only yesterday. Days as a shadow is a stock image of a short life.
b: The Hebrew is just "we are yesterday," meaning we arrived only yesterday and know little. Our days are "a shadow," the common biblical picture for a life that passes quickly (14:2; Psalm 144:4; 1 Chronicles 29:15; Ecclesiastes 6:12). Bildad uses the brevity of life to argue for humility before tradition. Job will use the same image of the shadow in 14:2 to argue the opposite: because life is so short, God should leave a man alone.

a: Without a marsh, can papyrus rise high?
p: Two Nile-marsh plants. The Hebrew uses Egyptian loanwords, and the picture is of growth that needs water.
b: Gome' is papyrus, the tall marsh plant of the Nile used for boats and paper (Exodus 2:3; Isaiah 18:2), and achu is a marsh grass; the word is borrowed from Egyptian and also appears in Genesis 41:2 for the reeds where Pharaoh's cows grazed. Bildad's proverb sounds like a saying from the schools of the wise: a plant without water dies early, even before ordinary grass, and so does a person cut off from God. Many think 8:11–19 quotes traditional sayings, the "words from their hearts" that he promised in 8:10.

a: That is the road of everyone who forgets God
p: The Hebrew says 'so are the paths of'. The Greek has 'so is the end of', which many scholars prefer.
b: The received Hebrew reads ken orchot, "so are the paths of all who forget God." The Greek has houtōs toinyn estai ta eschata, "so will be the end of all who forget the Lord," which seems to reflect 'acharit, "end, latter part." Several scholars (Dhorme, Clines) prefer that reading, since it fits Bildad's picture of the plant's sudden end and picks up his own word 'acharit in 8:7 ("your later years"). Proverbs 1:19 has a close parallel with "paths" ("such are the paths of everyone greedy for gain"), which supports the Hebrew. The Plain keeps "road," the received text.
orig: כֵּן אָרְחוֹת (ken orchot), 'so are the paths'

a: the godless man's hope will be lost
p: The KJV's 'hypocrite' is too narrow. Chanef means godless or profane, a person cut off from God.
b: The KJV renders chanef "hypocrite" here and often in Job, following the Greek of some books and the Latin hypocrita. The Hebrew word is wider and stronger: a person who is profane, godless, polluted (Isaiah 9:17; Jeremiah 23:11). Bildad is not accusing Job of play-acting, but placing him near those who "forget God." The word comes back at 13:16, where Job turns it around: a godless man would not dare to stand before God, but Job will.

a: His confidence snaps
p: The verb is found only here. 'Snaps' or 'is cut' is a guess from context; others think of a thread or gossamer.
b: Yaqot occurs only here, and its meaning is guessed. The old versions took it as "be cut off" (KJV), linked with quts. Some interpreters, medieval and modern, connected it with qayits, "summer," and read "summer threads," that is, gossamer, so that the line would mean "his confidence is gossamer," which fits the spider's house in the next line. The Greek reads quite differently: "his house will be uninhabited." Whatever the word, the picture is clear: what the godless lean on is as fragile as a web.

a: what he trusts is a spider's house
p: A web looks like a house but cannot bear any weight. Bildad's picture of false security.
b: Bildad keeps the word "house": the spider's house (8:14), the house he leans on (8:15), the house of stones (8:17). A web looks like a home and holds its maker up, but it breaks as soon as a person leans on it. The Qur'an uses the same picture for those who take protectors other than God: "the frailest of houses is the spider's house" (Qur'an 29:41). Isaiah also compares the works of the wicked to spider webs that cannot be worn as clothes (Isaiah 59:5–6). Job, whose house fell on his children (1:19), hears this pointedly.

a: Look at him in the sunshine, green and full of sap
p: Scholars disagree whether 8:16–19 describes a second wicked man, or a righteous man who is replanted.
b: Most commentators read 8:16–19 as a second picture of the godless: a lush plant whose roots seem secure among the stones, but which is torn out and forgotten (8:18), and others grow in its place (8:19). The Greek takes it so: "such is the overthrow of the ungodly." Some (Habel, following older Jewish readers) think the plant is the righteous man, who may be uprooted but sprouts again "from the dust" (8:19). That reading anticipates Job's own image of the tree that has hope (14:7–9). The Hebrew allows both; the sharper irony of 8:19 favors the first.

a: he looks out on a house of rocks
p: The Hebrew is obscure. A small change gives 'he holds fast to', and the Greek has 'he will live among pebbles'.
b: The Hebrew says the plant "sees a house of stones," which is hard to picture. Many scholars change one letter of yechezeh, "sees," to read yochez or yechezaq, "grasps, holds fast," so the roots grip the rocks. The Greek says "he lives in the midst of pebbles." The Plain keeps the Hebrew as written, which can mean the plant looks out on a stony place where it has taken root.
orig: בֵּית אֲבָנִים יֶחֱזֶה (beit avanim yechezeh), 'a house of stones he sees'

a: Yet if someone rips him out of his place
p: The verb is 'swallow', the same word used of God in 2:3 and by Job in 10:8.
b: Literally "if he (or someone) swallows it from its place." The verb billa', "swallow, destroy," is the word God used in the heavenly court: "you lured me against him, to swallow him up for no reason" (2:3). Job will use it of God in 10:8, "now you swallow me up." Bildad's uprooted plant is unknowingly Job's own story. Even the plant's place forgets it, an image of total loss in a culture that hoped to be remembered (7:10; Psalm 103:16).

a: that is the joy his road leads to
p: Bitter irony: 'that is the joy of his way'. The Greek read a different word: 'that is the overthrow of the ungodly'.
b: The Hebrew mesos darko, "the joy of his way," is sarcastic: this is all the joy the godless get. Some scholars think mesos is a mistake for a word meaning "rotting" or "melting" (from masas), which the Greek may reflect with katastrophē, "overthrow." Either way the point is the same: the plant dies and others replace it.
orig: מְשׂוֹשׂ דַּרְכּוֹ (mesos darko), 'the joy of his way'

a: God does not reject the wholehearted
p: Bildad uses tam, God's word for Job (1:1). Job answers, 'I am wholehearted... I reject my life' (9:21).
b: Tam is the word the narrator and God used for Job (1:1; 1:8; 2:3), rendered "wholehearted" there: a person of integrity, all of one piece. Bildad's rule sounds safe: God does not reject such a person. The reader, who heard God say Job is tam, knows Bildad has stated the very case the book is testing. Job seizes both words in reply: "I am wholehearted" (tam), "I reject (em'as) my life" (9:21), and "wholehearted or wicked, he finishes them off" (9:22). The Plain keeps "wholehearted" in all these verses so the echo of 1:1 stays visible; in chapter 9 the word also has a courtroom sense, "innocent, without fault."

a: He will still fill your mouth with laughing
p: The Hebrew begins 'until'. Most translators read it as 'yet' or 'still' by changing one vowel letter.
b: The verse begins with 'ad, "until," which does not join well with 8:20. Most scholars read 'od, "still, yet," by adding one small letter, vav (עד to עוד), and the Plain follows that sense. A few defend "until" as meaning that God will keep holding the blameless until he has filled his mouth with laughter. The picture of a mouth full of laughter is the joy of restoration in Psalm 126:2.
orig: עַד־יְמַלֵּה שְׂחוֹק פִּיךָ ('ad-yemalleh sechoq pikha), 'until he fills your mouth with laughter'

a: the tent of the wicked will not be there
p: Bildad's last word, 'is not', is the word Job used of himself in 7:21: 'I will not be there.'
b: The speech ends with 'enennu, "it is not, it will not be there." Job had ended his last speech with the same word about himself: "You will search hard for me, and I will not be there" (7:21). Bildad seems to answer him: it is not you who will vanish, but the wicked, if you are righteous. The tent of the wicked is a stock picture of a household that comes to nothing (18:14–15; Proverbs 14:11).

a: But how can a mortal be in the right with God?
p: Job takes up Eliphaz's question (4:17), but turns it into a legal one: how can anyone win a lawsuit against God?
b: Eliphaz asked, "Is any mortal in the right in God's sight?" (4:17), meaning that no creature is pure before God. Job agrees ("Yes, I know it is so"), but he hears the verb tsadaq in its courtroom sense: to be declared in the right, to win one's case. His question is not "how can a sinner be forgiven?" (the way Christians often read this verse, compare Romans 3:20–26) but "how can anyone win a trial against an opponent who is also the judge?" From here on Job speaks in the language of the law court: case, answer, summon, judge, guilty, innocent, umpire.

a: Suppose a man wanted to argue his case with him
p: The Hebrew does not say who would not answer. A man could not answer God, or God would not answer a man.
b: Lariv means to bring a lawsuit (riv). The second line, "he could not answer him one in a thousand," has no named subject. It may mean that a human could not answer one of God's thousand questions (the Greek and most translators take it so), or that God would not answer once in a thousand times. Habel and others think the ambiguity is deliberate. Both come true: God never answers Job's summons in the dialogue, and when he does speak (38–41) he asks questions Job cannot answer. The second line is one of the few places in chapters 8–14 where the Greek may not be Old Greek: Ziegler's Göttingen edition marks 9:3b with Origen's asterisk (a line supplied from Theodotion), while Pietersma and Gentry argue it belongs to the original translation (Gentry, Asterisked Materials). Elsewhere in these chapters the Greek covers nearly every line; its large gaps come later in the book.

a: He picks up mountains and moves them
p: 9:5–10 reads like a hymn to the Creator, but Job sings it as a complaint: this power is terrifying, not comforting.
b: Verses 5–10 use the form of Israel's hymns of praise, a string of participles: "the one who moves... who shakes... who speaks to the sun..." (compare Amos 4:13; Amos 5:8–9; Psalm 104). Eliphaz had used the same form to urge Job to trust God (5:9–16). Job keeps the form but changes its feeling. God's power over mountains, earth, sun and stars is real, but it is the power of anger (9:5), and it is exactly why no human can face him in court. Many scholars call this a parody of the hymn; others prefer to call it a lament that borrows the hymn's words.

a: the pillars under it shudder
p: The ancient picture of the world: the earth stands on pillars over the deep, and God can shake them.
b: Israel, like its neighbors, pictured the earth as resting on pillars or foundations sunk in the waters below (1 Samuel 2:8; Psalm 75:3; Psalm 104:5). An earthquake was God shaking those pillars. The language is the common picture of the world in that time, used here to show God's power, not as a lesson in geology. Job's own world has been shaken to its foundations.

a: He gives the sun an order, and it stays dark
t: A rare word for the sun
p: The word here is cheres, an uncommon poetic name for the sun, not the usual shemesh.
b: Cheres is a rare word for the sun (Judges 8:13; Judges 14:18). God can tell the sun not to rise and can "seal up" the stars, that is, shut them away so they do not shine. Job is not describing an eclipse but the Creator's ability to reverse creation, as he himself had wished his birth night to be dark (3:4–9). The Greek has "who commands the sun, and it does not rise."

a: tramples on the back of the Sea
p: 'The back of Yam': Yam, the Sea, was a monster god in Canaanite myth. God treads on him like a conqueror.
b: Bamotei yam means "the heights" or "the back of the Sea." In the texts from Ugarit, the god Baal defeats Yam, the Sea, a monster god of chaos. To tread on an enemy's back was the victor's gesture (Deuteronomy 33:29; Amos 4:13). Job, like the psalms and prophets, borrows the picture to say that the LORD alone, not Baal, is master of the chaotic sea (38:8–11; Psalm 74:13–14). The Bible does not take over the myth: the Sea is not a rival god but a creature God controls. The Greek has "walks on the sea as on dry ground," a line Christian readers recall in Jesus walking on the water (Mark 6:48–50).

a: The Bear is his work, and Orion, and the Pleiades
p: The names 'Ash, Kesil and Kimah are star groups, probably the Bear (or the Lion), Orion and the Pleiades.
b: The same names come back in God's speech: "Can you tie the knots that hold the Pleiades, / or untie the ropes of Orion?" (38:31; compare Amos 5:8). Kesil means "fool" and was probably Orion, pictured as a giant bound in the sky. Kimah (a "cluster") is probably the Pleiades. 'Ash (in 38:32 'ayish) is the hardest: older translations gave "Arcturus" (KJV); many now prefer the Great Bear, while some think of Aldebaran or the Lion. The Greek here lists "the Pleiades and Hesperus (the evening star) and Arcturus." "The rooms of the south" are probably the southern star fields hidden below the horizon.

a: He does great things, beyond searching out
p: This verse repeats Eliphaz's line in 5:9 almost word for word. Job agrees, and draws the opposite conclusion.
b: Eliphaz said, "He does great things, beyond searching out, / marvels that no one can count" (5:9), and urged Job to turn to so great a God. Job repeats the line almost exactly, then adds the next verse: God's wonders include passing by unseen (9:11) and snatching away with no one to stop him (9:12). The same truth about God's greatness becomes comfort in Eliphaz's mouth and terror in Job's. The Plain renders both verses alike to show the quotation.

a: He could walk right past me and I would not see
p: 'Pass by' recalls God passing Moses and Elijah, but Job sees nothing.
b: God "passing by" ('avar) is the language of revelation: the LORD passed by Moses and proclaimed his name (Exodus 33:19–22; Exodus 34:6) and passed by Elijah at Horeb (1 Kings 19:11). Eliphaz said a spirit "passed" before his face (4:15). For Job the passing brings no vision at all: God goes by, too great to be seen or grasped, and Job cannot tell what he is doing. Job will say the same in 23:8–9.

a: Who will ask him, 'What are you doing?'
p: The question echoes the language of royal power. Isaiah, Ecclesiastes, Daniel and Paul use the same question.
b: "What are you doing?" is the question no subject could put to a king (Ecclesiastes 8:4). The prophets and wise men use it of God: the clay cannot ask the potter what he is making (Isaiah 45:9), and none can stay God's hand and ask him "What have you done?" (Daniel 4:35). Paul takes up the same image (Romans 9:20). For those writers it calls for trust. For Job it states the problem: a power that no one may question is a power that no one can hold to account.

a: Rahab's helpers crouched down under him
p: Rahab is a sea monster of chaos, not Rahab of Jericho. Her 'helpers' are the monster's allies in the old battle story.
b: Rahab ("the arrogant one") is a name for the chaos monster of the sea (26:12; Psalm 89:10; Isaiah 51:9) and, by extension, for Egypt (Isaiah 30:7; Psalm 87:4). It is spelled differently in Hebrew from Rahab of Jericho (Joshua 2:1). Her "helpers" recall the allies of the monster Tiamat in the Babylonian creation story, who were taken captive when Marduk defeated her (Enuma Elish, tablet 4). Job means that even the cosmic monsters bowed to God's anger, so what hope has he? The Greek reads "the sea monsters under heaven bent down beneath him." The KJV, following medieval readings of rahab as "pride," has "the proud helpers."

a: I could only beg the one who judges me to be kind
p: The form means 'my opponent at law' or 'my judge'. Job's point is that in God's case they are the same.
b: Limshofti is an unusual form of the verb "to judge" (a poel participle), found only here. It can mean "my judge" or "the one who goes to law with me, my adversary." Job's problem is that God would be both: the other party in the case and the one who decides it. Even if he were right, he could only beg for mercy (ethannan, the word Bildad used in 8:5). Bildad told him to plead; Job says pleading is all a man could do, guilty or not.

a: He is the one who bruises me in a windstorm
p: Job uses two words the reader knows: God will answer him from this very 'storm' (38:1), and 'for no reason' is 2:3.
b: Two words in this line reach across the book. Se'arah, "storm," is the word for the windstorm from which the LORD answers Job (38:1; 40:6). And chinnam, "for no reason," is the Accuser's word ("Is it for no reason that Job fears God?" 1:9) and God's ("to swallow him up for no reason," 2:3). Job does not know about the heavenly scene, but he names it exactly. The Talmud says Job complained, "Perhaps a stormwind passed before you, and you confused Iyov (Job) with oyev (enemy)," and that God answered from the storm that he does not confuse even one hair with another (Bava Batra 16a), a play on se'arah and sa'arah, "hair."

a: Who will name me a day in court?
p: The Hebrew says 'who will summon me?' Many think it should be 'him', as the Greek suggests. See the variant.
b: Yo'ideni means "will set a time for me, summon me" (as in Jeremiah 49:19). In the mouth of Job it is odd, since Job is the one who wants to summon God. Some scholars hear Job quoting God's own voice: "Who will summon me?" Others read "him" (yo'idennu), which the Greek seems to support: "who will stand against his judgment?" Either way, there is no court above God where Job can bring his case.
orig: מִי יוֹעִידֵנִי (mi yo'ideni), 'who will summon me?'

a: I no longer know myself
p: Literally 'I do not know my soul'. Job may mean 'I no longer care about myself' or 'I am beside myself'.
b: Lo eda' nafshi is literally "I do not know my nefesh (self, life)." It may mean "I do not care about my life," which leads to "I reject my life"; or "I am out of my mind"; or "I cannot know whether I am guilty" (the Greek: "whether I sinned, I do not know in my soul"). What is clear is the claim before it: tam ani, "I am wholehearted," the very word God used of Job (1:8; 2:3). He holds to his integrity even while he despairs of his life.

a: wholehearted or wicked, he finishes them off
p: The heart of Job's protest: God destroys the good and the wicked alike.
b: Job says what the friends will never say: there is no moral difference in how God treats people. Readers have taken this line in three main ways. Some (many Christian and Jewish moralists) see it as the sin of Job's words, the overreach that God later rebukes (38:2; 40:8). Others (Clines, Newsom) take it as the honest report of what Job sees, which the book lets stand and God never refutes point by point; Ecclesiastes says something similar (Ecclesiastes 9:2–3). On the Talmud's debate over Job's next words, see the note on 9:24. Here tam is again "wholehearted," God's own word for Job (1:1; 2:3): Job puts himself in the group God destroys.

a: the innocent despair, and he scoffs at them
p: The noun massah may come from 'melt' (despair) or from 'test' (trial, KJV). Either way God is pictured laughing.
b: Massat neqiyyim is either "the melting (despair) of the innocent" (from masas, "to melt") or "the testing of the innocent" (from nasah, "to test"; KJV "trial"). The second would be a striking hint at the test of chapters 1–2, though Job does not know of it. The picture of God mocking is one of the harshest in the Bible. Proverbs uses the same verb for Wisdom laughing at fools in their disaster (Proverbs 1:26); Job applies it to the innocent.

a: If he is not the one, then who is?
p: Job refuses to blame chance or a lesser power. Readers who know of the Accuser hear an unknowing question.
b: Job sees injustice in the world: a land in a wicked man's power, judges blindfolded so they cannot see what is right. He refuses every escape: if God is not doing it, who is? The reader knows the Accuser from chapters 1–2 and may want to answer for Job. But the prologue itself has God say that the Accuser "lured me against him" (2:3): the book does not let God off the hook by blaming the Accuser. The Talmud (Bava Batra 16a) records a debate over whether Job here speaks of God or of the Accuser; Rashi takes "the wicked one" in the first line as the Accuser.

a: They glide away with the papyrus boats
p: The 'ships of 'eveh' are probably light papyrus boats, the fastest craft of the Nile.
b: 'Oniyyot 'eveh appears only here. Most scholars connect 'eveh with a word for reed or papyrus (compare Akkadian apu, "reed, reed thicket"), so these are the light reed skiffs that skimmed along the Nile (Isaiah 18:2). The Greek has "is there a track of a ship's path?" Job piles up the swiftest things he knows: a royal runner on land (9:25), a reed boat on water, an eagle in the air. His life is going by faster than any of them.

a: So why wear myself out for a puff of air?
p: Hevel, 'breath, vapor', is the key word of Ecclesiastes. Job has already called his days hevel (7:16).
b: Job had said, "my days are a puff of air" (7:16). Now he says any effort to clear his name is hevel: breath, vapor, something that vanishes. Ecclesiastes uses the same word 38 times ("Breath of breaths... all is breath," Ecclesiastes 1:2), traditionally rendered "vanity." Job's sense is not "meaningless" in general, but "useless": the verdict has been decided before the trial begins.
orig: הֶבֶל אִיגָע (hevel iga'), 'for breath I labor'

a: made my hands clean with lye
p: Lye (borit) was a cleansing alkali made from plant ash. Washing the hands was also a public sign of innocence.
b: Bor (elsewhere borit) was an alkali made from the ashes of certain plants and used as soap (Jeremiah 2:22; Malachi 3:2). Washing the hands in public declared a person innocent of blood (Deuteronomy 21:6–7; Psalm 26:6; Matthew 27:24). Job means that no ritual of innocence would help him: God would plunge him back into the pit (9:31). David prayed to be made "whiter than snow" (Psalm 51:7); Job says snow would not be enough.
orig: בְּבֹר כַּפָּי (bevor kappai), 'with lye my hands'
r: Jeremiah 2:22; Malachi 3:2; Deuteronomy 21:6–7; Psalm 26:6; Psalm 51:7; Isaiah 1:18; Matthew 27:24

a: my own clothes would be disgusted with me
p: A bold image: the clean clothes refuse to touch the man God has dipped in filth.
b: The pit (shachat) here is a muddy hole or sewer; the Greek has "filth." Job imagines that after he has scrubbed himself, God would dip him back in the muck so thoroughly that his own clothes would recoil from him. Some scholars change "my clothes" (salmotay) to "my friends," but no ancient witness supports this, and the image of clothes is striking enough on its own. Compare Zechariah 3:3–5, where the high priest's filthy clothes are taken away by God.

a: He is no human like me, someone I could answer back
p: Job's dilemma: a fair trial needs two equal parties and a judge above both. With God there is neither.
b: Job has worked out the problem with great clarity. A lawsuit needs two parties on the same level and a court that can decide between them. God is not a human whom Job can meet in court; he is the other party, the judge, and the power that can crush the plaintiff. Ancient Near Eastern sufferers, like the Babylonian poem "I Will Praise the Lord of Wisdom" (Ludlul), also complain that the gods' ways are hidden, but they do not imagine taking a god to court. Job's legal imagination is new, and it shapes the whole book (13:3; 23:3–7; 31:35–37).

a: If only someone stood between us to judge the case
p: Mokhiach: one who decides between two parties. Job wishes for one; the standard Hebrew says there is none.
b: Mokhiach comes from yakach, "to argue, decide, set right." It is the third party who hears both sides and settles the dispute (Genesis 31:37; Isaiah 2:4, "He will be judge between the nations and set things right for many peoples"), an umpire or arbiter. Laying a hand on each party may picture a judge's authority over both, or a go-between bringing them together. The KJV's "daysman" was an old English word for an umpire who set a day for a hearing. The Plain reads the line as a wish, "if only," with the Greek, the Syriac and some Hebrew manuscripts; the received Hebrew says flatly "there is no" such person (see the variant). Either way Job has no one. The same root returns in 13:3, 13:15 and 16:21, and his longing grows: someone to judge between them here, a witness in heaven in 16:19, and a redeemer (go'el) in 19:25.

a: to put his hand on each of us
p: The Greek calls this figure a 'mediator'. Christian readers heard Christ, the one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5).
b: The Greek renders mokhiach with mesitēs, "mediator," the word Paul uses: "God is one, and one also is the mediator between God and humans: Christ Jesus, himself human" (1 Timothy 2:5). Gregory the Great and many later preachers read Job's longing as a cry that only the incarnation answers: one who is both God and human can lay a hand on both. Jewish readers (Rashi, Ibn Ezra) take the figure as Job's wish for a fair human-style court; some medieval and modern readers think of an angelic advocate like the one Elihu describes (33:23–24). Critical scholars read Job's words as the logic of a lawsuit, not a prophecy, while many note how naturally they open toward later hopes. The verse itself says only that Job has no one, and wishes he had.

a: Let him lift his rod off me
p: Either the hoped-for judge would take God's rod off Job, or Job asks God himself to lift it.
b: If "him" is the one Job wishes for in 9:33, Job pictures a go-between who would take God's rod away so that Job could speak without fear (so the NIV reading). If "him" is God, Job asks God directly to stop beating him so that a fair hearing is possible. The same request comes back in 13:21, addressed to God: "pull your hand back, far off me, / and let your terror stop frightening me." That parallel favors reading 9:34 as about God.

a: because inside myself I am not that way
p: Literally 'for not so am I with myself'. It may mean 'I am not afraid at heart' or 'I am not guilty as he treats me'.
b: The Hebrew ki lo-khen anokhi 'immadi is very compressed. Proposals: (1) "I am not like that inside," meaning Job knows he is not the guilty man God treats him as; the Greek has "for I am not conscious of anything like that"; (2) "it is not so with me," meaning that as things are, Job cannot speak freely (the NIV takes it so); (3) "I am not afraid deep down," so if the terror were lifted he would speak boldly. The Plain keeps the literal shape, which leaves these options open.
orig: כִּי לֹא־כֵן אָנֹכִי עִמָּדִי (ki lo-khen anokhi 'immadi)

a: I will talk out of the bitterness inside me
p: Literally 'in the bitterness of my nefesh'. Job will not hide what he feels; he lets his complaint go.
b: Bemar nafshi, "in the bitterness of my soul," repeats 7:11 and recalls Hannah's prayer "bitter of soul" (1 Samuel 1:10). Siach, "complaint," is the word of the lament psalms (Psalm 142:2). The verb 'azav, "let loose, let go," is the same verb Job used in 9:27 ("drop this face"): there he imagined giving up his complaint; here he gives up on silence instead. Chapter 10 is addressed to God, the first long prayer of the book.

a: Let me know what your case against me is about
p: Job asks for the basic right of an accused man: to hear the charge. The verb is riv, 'bring a lawsuit'.
b: Al-mah teriveni, "on what grounds do you bring a lawsuit against me?" uses riv, the lawsuit word of 9:3. In Israelite law a person was not condemned without witnesses and a stated charge (Deuteronomy 19:15–18). Job does not yet ask God to admit he is innocent; he asks first for the indictment. He asks again in 13:23 ("Make my rebellion and my sin known to me"), and the request is never directly answered.

a: to toss aside what your own hands worked so hard to make
p: Literally 'the toil of your palms'. Job reminds God that he is God's own handiwork, a theme that runs through 10:3–12.
b: Yegia' kappekha is "the labor of your palms," what a craftsman has worked hard to make. The same verb "reject" (ma'as) appeared in 8:20 and 9:21. Job asks why God would make something with care and then throw it away. The theme of God as craftsman comes back in 10:8–12 and 14:15 ("you would yearn for the thing your hands had made"), and in the prayers of Israel: "the works of your hands, do not let them fall" (Psalm 138:8).

a: Are your eyes made of flesh?
p: Job asks whether God sees like a human, with limited sight that must search for evidence. The answer should be no.
b: Job's questions in 10:4–7 are a sharp argument. A human judge, with "eyes of flesh" and a short life, must dig for evidence before time runs out. But God sees everything and lives forever (compare 1 Samuel 16:7, "A human sees what is before the eyes, but the LORD sees the heart"). So why does God hunt for Job's sin (10:6) as though he needed to find it, when he already knows Job is not guilty (10:7)? Rashi reads the questions as Job asking God not to judge him by appearances.

a: even though you know I am not a wicked man
p: The rabbis read this verse as Job's boldest argument: God made both the righteous and the wicked.
b: The Babylonian Talmud (Bava Batra 16a) records Rava's reading: with these words Job "tried to free the whole world from judgment." He said to God that God created the ox with split hooves and the donkey without, the Garden of Eden and Gehinnom, the righteous and the wicked, so who can stop his hand? Job's friends, Rava says, answered him that God also created the impulse to evil and the Torah as its remedy. The passage shows how seriously the rabbis took Job's protest, and how they argued with it from within the tradition.

a: Your hands molded me and made me
p: The verb 'itsev means to shape, as a sculptor shapes. God's hands are the craftsman's hands of Genesis 2.
b: The verb 'itsev, "shape, fashion," is used of a potter or sculptor (Jeremiah 44:19). Job's words recall how "the LORD God shaped the man from dust of the ground" (Genesis 2:7), and they introduce one of the most tender passages in the book (10:8–12). But each tender line turns bitter. The verse ends "and you swallow me up," the verb God used of himself in 2:3. On the Hebrew of "every part of me," see the variant.

a: And now you will send me back to the dust?
p: Job joins two creation pictures: the potter and his clay, and the dust humans return to (Genesis 3:19).
b: Chomer is potter's clay. The prophets use the potter to say God may reshape his people as he likes (Isaiah 64:8; Jeremiah 18:1–6); Job uses it to ask why a potter would smash his own vessel. The return to dust is God's word to Adam, "to dust you will go back" (Genesis 3:19), and Job's own (1:21; 7:21). Elihu later answers this verse: "I too was nipped off from clay" (33:6).

a: Like cheese you made me thicken
t: Milk and cheese: forming in the womb
p: An ancient picture of conception: the seed is poured like milk and sets like cheese, then flesh and bones are added.
b: Many ancient peoples imagined a child forming as milk curdles into cheese: the father's seed is poured out, the mother's blood thickens it, and it slowly sets. Aristotle uses the same comparison (Generation of Animals 2.4), and the Wisdom of Solomon, Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians, describes a body "carved into flesh over a time of ten months, set firm in blood" (Wisdom of Solomon 7:1–2). Job's lines (10:10–11) are the Bible's fullest picture of the body forming before birth, beside Psalm 139:13–16 and Ecclesiastes 11:5. The point is God's personal care in every stage.
r: Psalm 139:13–16; Ecclesiastes 11:5; Wisdom of Solomon 7:1–2; 2 Maccabees 7:22–23; Jeremiah 1:5

a: You worked life and loyal love for me
p: Job admits that God once showed him hesed, loyal love, and guarded his breath. That makes the present harder to bear.
b: Hesed, rendered "loyal love" across this site, is the faithful kindness of a covenant partner (Exodus 34:6). Pequddah is God's watchful care, his "visiting" for good (the KJV has "thy visitation"). In 7:18 Job complained that God "visits" him every morning to test him; here the same root names the care that kept him alive. The memory of God's past love is the root of Job's pain: the same God who formed and protected him now seems to hunt him (10:16).

a: But all along you kept these things hidden in your heart
p: Job accuses God of planning his suffering all along. Something was hidden, but not what Job thinks.
b: "These things" probably points forward to 10:14–17: while God was forming and protecting Job, he was already planning to watch him and punish him. Job sees a cruel secret purpose behind the care. The reader knows there was a hidden purpose, the test of chapters 1–2, but it is not the one Job imagines. Gregory the Great read the verse as Job's recognition that God's mercies and judgments are both stored in his counsel. Many modern readers see it as the darkest line in Job's speech.

a: I have had my fill of shame, and I look at my misery
p: The Hebrew says 'see my affliction'. Many scholars change one letter to read 'soaked in my affliction'.
b: The line has two parallel phrases: seva' qalon, "full of shame," and re'eh 'onyi, "see my affliction." Because "see" breaks the parallel, many scholars read reveh, "soaked, drenched" (one letter different), giving "full of shame and soaked in affliction." Others keep the Hebrew as an imperative to God, "see my affliction!" (KJV), or, as the Plain does, as Job looking at his own misery. The Greek has only "for I am full of dishonor."
orig: שְׂבַע קָלוֹן וּרְאֵה עָנְיִי (seva' qalon ur'eh 'onyi)

a: you track me down like a lion
p: Job reverses a familiar image. In the psalms the wicked hunt like lions; here God is the lion and Job the prey.
b: In the lament psalms the enemies are lions stalking the righteous (Psalm 7:2; Psalm 17:12), and God rescues him. Hosea and Lamentations dare to picture God himself as a lion or bear tearing his people (Hosea 5:14; Hosea 13:7–8; Lamentations 3:10). Job takes that bold picture further: God's "wonders" (the word used of his saving acts, Exodus 3:20) are now shown "at my expense." Eliphaz had spoken of the lion's teeth being broken (4:10–11); Job feels himself in the lion's mouth.

a: one shift of soldiers after another is against me
p: Literally 'changes and an army'. Many read the pair as one idea: fresh troops in relays.
b: Chalifot vetsava, "changes and a host," is probably a pair that means one thing: troops sent in waves, a fresh shift relieving the last (compare 1 Kings 5:14, shifts of workers). The "witnesses" ('edekha) in the first line keep the courtroom picture; some read 'adekha, "your attacks," by a small change. Tsava returns in 14:14 for Job's own hard service, and chalifah for his longed-for relief. The KJV's "changes and war" is literal but obscure.

a: So why did you bring me out of the womb?
p: Job returns to his first lament: it would have been better never to be born (3:11–16).
b: Chapter 3 was a curse on the day of Job's birth spoken to no one. Here Job asks the same question directly to God: "why?" Jeremiah asks it too (Jeremiah 20:14–18). The two passages differ in a telling way: in chapter 3 Job wishes the night had prevented his birth; here he says God is the one who brought him out. The complaint has become a charge against a person.

a: to the land of darkness and deep shadow
p: Tsalmavet was long read as 'shadow of death' (KJV, Psalm 23:4). Most scholars now read it as 'deep darkness'.
b: The Masoretes pointed tsalmavet as two words, tsel "shadow" and mavet "death," and the Greek, Latin and KJV render "shadow of death," as in Psalm 23:4. Many scholars think the word was originally tsalmut, "deep darkness," from a root known in Akkadian and Arabic. In Job it is used for the darkness of the underworld (here and 38:17), where both senses meet. In these chapters the Plain uses "deep shadow," as at 3:5; other parts of the book use "deep darkness" or "death-dark shadow" where the context leans one way.

a: and when it shines, it shines like gloom
p: Sheol is the undoing of creation: no order, and a 'light' that is only darkness. The Greek and Latin expand the verse.
b: God made the world by separating light from darkness and setting things in order (Genesis 1:3–5). Job pictures the land of the dead as creation run backward: "no order" (lo sedarim, the only use of the word in the Bible), and a dawn that is only gloom. The Greek has "a land of eternal darkness, where there is no light, nor seeing the life of mortals," and the Latin Vulgate adds "everlasting horror dwells there," a line that shaped later Christian pictures of hell. In the Hebrew Bible Sheol is the shadowy home of all the dead, not a place of punishment.

a: Zophar the Naamathite
p: The third friend. His home, Naamah, is unknown; a town in Judah had the name, but an Arabian site is more likely.
b: Zophar is named at 2:11. A town called Naamah lay in the lowlands of Judah (Joshua 15:41), but the friends seem to come from Edom and Arabia, so many look for an eastern site. The Greek calls him "Sophar the Minaean," king of the Minaeans, a people of southern Arabia. Zophar speaks only twice (11; 20); he has no speech in the third round, which is one sign that chapters 24–27 have been disturbed (see the 22–31 chapter pages).

a: Will a man who is all talk win his case?
p: Literally 'a man of lips'. Zophar takes Job's legal words and turns them on him: talking does not make you right.
b: Ish sefatayim, "a man of lips," is a chatterer. The verb yitsdaq, "be in the right, win a case," is the legal word Job used in 9:2 and 9:15. Zophar answers Job's lawsuit with contempt: many words do not win a case. The Greek adds a line from 14:1 here, "one born of woman, short-lived," perhaps a scribe's or translator's echo.

a: What I teach is spotless
p: Zophar puts words in Job's mouth that Job never quite said. Job claimed innocence, not perfect doctrine.
b: Leqach is "teaching, instruction" (Proverbs 4:2), and zakh "pure." Job never claimed his teaching was pure; he claimed that he had not denied God's words (6:10) and that he was blameless (9:21) and not wicked (10:7). Zophar's summary is a little unfair: he turns Job's claim of integrity into a claim of sinless perfection, which is easier to refute. The Greek even has Job say "I am blameless in deeds." Elihu will do the same in 33:9 ("I am pure and free of rebellion").

a: How I wish God himself would speak
t: Be careful what you wish for
p: Zophar wishes God would speak and rebuke Job. When God does speak (38–41), he rebukes the friends instead (42:7).
b: Zophar is sure that if God spoke, he would side with the friends. The book grants Zophar's wish in a way he did not expect. God does answer from the windstorm (38:1), and he challenges Job, but in the end the LORD says to Eliphaz, "You did not say what is right about me, the way my servant Job did" (42:7). Job himself has wished for a hearing (9:16; 13:22), and his wish is the one the book takes seriously.

a: since sound wisdom is twofold
p: A famously obscure line. 'Twofold' may mean wisdom has a hidden side, or is double what humans see.
b: Ki-khiflayim letushiyyah is literally "for double (or 'folds') to sound wisdom." Proposals: (1) wisdom has two sides, an open one and a hidden one, and God knows both; (2) God's wisdom is double, far greater than ours; (3) a slight change gives "for wonders (ki-fela'im) belong to wisdom" (Dhorme and others), which fits 11:7 well. The Greek has "it will be double of what is with you." Tushiyyah is practical wisdom that succeeds (5:12; Proverbs 2:7). The Plain keeps the Hebrew and its uncertainty.

a: God is letting part of your guilt be forgotten
p: Zophar says Job's suffering is milder than his sins. It is the harshest judgment any friend has spoken.
b: Yashsheh lekha Eloah me'avonekha is "God causes some of your guilt to be forgotten for you" (from nashah, "forget"). The KJV's "God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth" takes the verb from a root meaning "lend, demand payment," and gives the same sense: Job is getting off lightly. Zophar goes further than Eliphaz or Bildad. They hinted Job had sinned; Zophar says that whatever Job has suffered is less than he deserves. Ezra 9:13 uses the idea in a humble confession by the guilty; here it is a judgment passed on someone else. Maimonides saw Zophar as the voice of pure divine will: God does what he wills, and humans cannot ask why (Guide 3.23).
orig: כִּי־יַשֶּׁה לְךָ אֱלוֹהַ מֵעֲוֹנֶךָ (ki-yashsheh lekha Eloah me'avonekha)

a: Will you get to the bottom of God by searching?
p: Zophar's hymn on God's unsearchable wisdom (11:7–9) is echoed in Paul's praise in Romans 11:33.
b: Cheqer Eloah is "the searching (or depths) of God," and takhlit Shaddai "the limit of the Almighty." Zophar's point, that God is beyond human measure in every direction, is true, and God's speeches will say something like it (38–39). Paul sings it: "Oh, how deep are God's riches, his wisdom and his knowledge! No one can search out his judgments" (Romans 11:33). The problem is how Zophar uses it: as a reason Job must be guilty and must be quiet. Job will answer that he knows God's greatness as well as anyone (12:3; 12:13–25).

a: Deeper than Sheol! What can you know?
p: Height, depth, length and breadth: God's wisdom measured in every direction (compare Ephesians 3:18).
b: Zophar's four measures, the heights of heaven, deeper than Sheol, longer than the earth, broader than the sea (11:8–9), cover the whole cosmos as the ancients pictured it, from the sky above to the realm of the dead below. Psalm 139:8 uses the same high and low points for God's presence. Ephesians 3:18 prays that believers may grasp "the width and length and height and depth" of Christ's love, which many commentators connect with this verse. The Hebrew of the first line says "heights of the heavens," which many read, with a small change, as "higher than the heavens."

a: puts someone under arrest
p: Zophar borrows Job's words from 9:11–12: God is unstoppable, and Zophar calls that justice.
b: Zophar picks up Job's own words: God "passes through" (yachalof, 9:11) and "who will make him turn back?" (mi yeshivennu, 9:12). Job used them to complain that no one can hold God to account. Zophar uses them to say that when God arrests someone and calls the court to judge him, he is right to do so, because he sees evil directly (11:11). "Calls the assembly" (yaqhil) probably pictures a public trial before the community (Proverbs 5:14).

a: he sees evil, and he need not look twice
p: The Hebrew 'and he does not consider' may be a question (does he not notice?) or a statement (he need not study it).
b: Velo yitbonan is "and he does not consider." Read as a question, as the KJV, it means God surely takes note of evil. Read as a statement, it means God knows evil at once, without needing to examine it (so Rashi and many moderns), which is the point Job himself makes about God's eyes in 10:4–6. A third proposal changes the subject: humans see evil and do not consider it. The Plain follows the statement reading.

a: on the day a wild donkey's foal is born human
p: A pun: a 'hollow' man will get a 'heart' when a wild donkey gives birth to a human.
b: Ish navuv yillavev is a pun: a hollow (navuv) man will get heart (yillavev, from lev, heart, mind). The second line is probably a proverb for something that will never happen, as a wild donkey (pere) will never bear a human (adam). The same pair, pere adam, describes Ishmael: "He will be a wild donkey of a man" (Genesis 16:12). Others read the line as hope, "even a wild donkey's foal can be born again as a human," meaning a fool can be tamed. The Greek is quite different: man "swims about in words" and is "like a donkey of the desert." Either way Zophar is calling Job a fool.
orig: וְאִישׁ נָבוּב יִלָּבֵב וְעַיִר פֶּרֶא אָדָם יִוָּלֵד (ve'ish navuv yillavev ve'ayir pere adam yivvaled)

a: spread your palms out to him
p: The open palms were Israel's gesture of prayer, raised toward heaven or the Temple.
b: Israelites prayed standing with their palms open and lifted (Exodus 9:29; 1 Kings 8:22; 1 Kings 8:38; Psalm 143:6). Zophar's call to repentance has three steps: set the heart right, pray, and put away wrongdoing (11:13–14). It is good advice in itself, the advice of the prophets (Isaiah 1:15–17). Its fault is the assumption that Job has hidden wickedness "in his hand" and "in his tents."
r: Exodus 9:29; 1 Kings 8:22; 1 Kings 8:38; Psalm 143:6; Isaiah 1:15–17; Lamentations 3:41; 1 Timothy 2:8

a: set solid as cast metal
p: Mutsaq means 'poured, cast', like metal from a furnace: hard, firm, and secure.
b: Mutsaq is from yatsaq, "pour, cast," used of metal cast in a mold (1 Kings 7:23–24). Elihu will use the same word for the sky, "hard as a mirror cast from metal" (37:18). Zophar promises that a repentant Job would stand as firm as a casting. "Raise your face" answers Job directly: Job said that even if innocent he "cannot raise my head" (10:15).

a: if it grows dark, it will turn into morning
p: Zophar answers Job's picture of the land of darkness (10:21–22): repent, and even your darkness will be dawn.
b: Job ended his last speech in "the land of darkness and deep shadow" (10:21–22). Zophar promises the reverse: a life brighter than noon, and darkness itself turned to morning. The verb ta'ufah is hard: it may mean "(if) it is dark" from 'ufah, "darkness," or "you will fly up," which some versions take as "you will shine." The Greek has "your prayer will be like the morning star." The prophets use the same hope (Isaiah 58:10; Psalm 37:6).

a: you will search your place and sleep without a care
p: The verb chafar means 'dig' or 'search out'. Here it likely means looking around your home and finding it safe.
b: Vechafarta can mean "you will dig" (KJV, perhaps for water or a tent peg) or "you will search," as one checks a camp at night before lying down. A different root with the same letters means "be ashamed," which does not fit here. The Plain follows "search." The picture is the shepherd's security that Eliphaz also promised (5:24).

a: all they can hope for is to breathe out their life
p: Zophar ends with a warning that answers Job's wish to die: for the wicked, the only 'hope' is their last breath.
b: Mappach nefesh is "a breathing out of life," the last breath at death (compare Jeremiah 15:9). Job had longed for death (6:8–9; 7:15). Zophar's last line implies that a man who hopes for death is speaking like the wicked. The eyes that "wear out" (tikhlenah) are eyes that fail from looking for help that never comes (17:5; Deuteronomy 28:32). Zophar's speech ends, like Bildad's, with the fate of the wicked as a warning.

a: Truly, you are the people!
p: Job's reply opens with sarcasm: 'You are the people', as if all wisdom lived and would die in them.
b: Ki attem-'am, "you are the people," is biting irony. Some scholars think 'am here means "people who count, the people of standing," or read it as a shortened form "you are the people who know." The second line makes the tone plain: "wisdom will die when you do." Job answers Zophar's "hollow man" (11:12) by mocking the friends' claim to own the tradition (8:8–10).

a: My own friend laughs at me
p: A man whose prayers God once answered is now a joke, and so is every righteous man.
b: Sechoq, "laughingstock," frames the verse at both ends. Job describes himself as "one who called to God and he answered him": a man known for his prayers being heard. Now he is a joke to his friends, and a righteous, wholehearted man has become a joke in general. Early Christian readers (Gregory the Great) read the verse as a picture of the righteous mocked by the world, and of Christ mocked on the cross (Matthew 27:39–44). Job's word tamim here is close to tam, the word God used of him (1:1).

a: The comfortable man looks down on bad luck
p: The KJV saw a 'lamp despised'. Most now read 'for disaster, contempt': the comfortable despise the unlucky.
b: The first word, lappid, can be read as "torch, lamp" (KJV "a lamp despised") or divided as le-fid, "for disaster" (pid, as in 30:24; 31:29). Most scholars take the second: in the mind of one at ease there is contempt for misfortune. The second line, nakhon lemo'adei ragel, may mean "it is ready for those whose feet slip" or, reading nakhon from nakah, "a blow for those whose feet slip." Either way Job describes the attitude of his friends: those who are safe assume the fallen deserve their fall. The Greek paraphrases freely.
orig: לַפִּיד בּוּז לְעַשְׁתּוּת שַׁאֲנָן (lappid buz le'ashtut sha'anan)

a: people who carry their god in their own hand
p: Obscure. It may mean the violent make their own power their god, or that God has put them in his hand.
b: La'asher hevi Eloah beyado is literally "to whom/who brings God in his hand." Three readings: (1) robbers whose god is their own fist or weapon, like the conqueror "whose own strength is his god" (Habakkuk 1:11); (2) those whom God has brought into his power, yet who prosper; (3) those who carry idols. Many think the line is a later addition, since it makes the verse three lines long. The Plain follows (1), which suits the robbers of the first line.
orig: לַאֲשֶׁר הֵבִיא אֱלוֹהַּ בְּיָדוֹ (la'asher hevi Eloah beyado)

a: Just go and question the cattle, and let them teach you
p: Job sends the friends to school with the animals. What creation teaches is God's power, not his justice.
b: Wisdom often learns from animals (Proverbs 6:6; Proverbs 30:24–28). Job does the same, but with a twist. What the cattle, birds, earth and fish all know is that God's hand does everything (12:9), including the violence of the world where the strong eat the weak. Some scholars think Job quotes the friends' own lesson in 12:7–12 and then mocks it; others take it as his own claim that the order everyone can see is power without moral sense. God's speeches will send Job to the animals too (38:39–39:30), with a very different lesson.

a: Or have a talk with the ground
t: Talk to the earth, or the shrubs?
p: Siach is either 'speak to' or the noun 'shrub'. Some read 'the shrubs of the earth', to match the animals and fish.
b: Siach la'arets most naturally means "talk to the earth." But siach is also a noun, "shrub, bush" (Genesis 2:5; 30:4), and some read "the shrubs of the earth will teach you," which completes the list of living things: beasts, birds, plants, fish. The KJV and the Plain keep the verb.

a: that it was the LORD's hand that did this
p: YHWH, the LORD, appears only here in the poetic debate (3:1–42:6, outside the headings). The line quotes Isaiah 41:20.
b: Everywhere else in the speeches of Job and his friends, God is called El, Eloah or Shaddai, names that suit speakers outside Israel. Only here does the divine name YHWH appear (the narrator uses it in the prologue, in 38:1, 40:1–6 and 42:1, and in the epilogue). The words "the hand of the LORD has done this" are found exactly in Isaiah 41:20, and many scholars think Job (or a scribe) is quoting a well-known line. A number of Hebrew manuscripts read Eloah here instead; see the variant. The Greek has kyrios, "Lord," which supports YHWH.

a: and the breath in every human body
p: Nefesh and ruach, life and breath, are in God's hand. Numbers calls him 'the God of the spirits of all flesh'.
b: Nefesh kol-chai, "the life of every living thing," and ruach kol-besar-ish, "the breath of all human flesh," recall Numbers 16:22 and Numbers 27:16 ("God of the spirits of all flesh") and Daniel 5:23 ("the God who holds your every breath in his hand"). The thought is common to all the speakers. Elihu repeats it: if God drew his breath back, "every living body would die at once" (34:14–15). For Job it means that his own life is in the same hand that is crushing him.

a: The ear puts words to the test, does it not
p: A proverb Elihu repeats almost word for word (34:3): words, like food, should be tasted before they are swallowed.
b: The palate (chekh) tastes food and decides whether to eat; so the ear should test what it hears. Job means the friends' traditional sayings should not be swallowed whole. Elihu uses the same proverb to introduce his own judgment ("For the ear puts words to the test, / just as the mouth tastes food to eat," 34:3). Wisdom literature often uses taste for discernment (Psalm 34:8; Proverbs 24:13–14).

a: The gray-haired have wisdom
t: Wisdom of the aged: statement or question?
p: A statement, a quotation to mock, or a question? The next verse puts all wisdom with God.
b: The Hebrew has no question marker, but questions without markers are common in Job. Three readings: (1) a plain statement of the common view that age brings wisdom (32:7; Proverbs 16:31); (2) a quotation of the friends, especially Eliphaz, who boasted of the gray-haired on his side (15:10), followed by Job's answer in 12:13 that real wisdom is God's; (3) a question, "Is wisdom with the aged?" (so the NIV). Elihu, the youngest speaker, will dispute the idea directly (32:6–9). The Greek has "in much time is wisdom."

a: But wisdom and strength live with him
p: Job's hymn to God's wisdom and power, in which nearly every act is destructive.
b: Job now offers his own hymn, matching the friends' praise of God (5:9–16; 11:7–9). Four qualities, wisdom (chokhmah), might (gevurah), counsel ('etsah) and understanding (tevunah), are claimed for God alone (compare Isaiah 11:2). Then come almost twenty acts, and nearly all overturn something: walls torn down, water held back or let loose, counselors stripped, kings bound, priests sent barefoot, nations destroyed. Some readers call it a hymn to God the destroyer. Some readers hear in it a history of Israel's exile, when its kings, priests and elders were led away (2 Kings 25:4–21). The first readers, living after that history, could hardly miss it.

a: he sends them out, and they overturn the earth
p: God can stop the water (drought) or release it (flood). Readers hear the stories of Elijah's drought and Noah's flood.
b: The verb "overturn" (hafakh) is the word for the overthrow of Sodom (Genesis 19:25) and for God overturning mountains (9:5). Withholding water recalls the drought of Elijah's time (1 Kings 17:1); releasing it, the Flood (Genesis 7:11). God controls rain and seas, the two great powers of life and death in the ancient Near East. In the speeches from the storm God asks Job whether he can do the same (38:25–38).

a: the one who strays and the one who leads him astray are both his
p: A hard line: both the deceived and the deceiver belong to God. Job says even error is under God's control.
b: Shogeg umashgeh, "the one who errs and the one who leads into error," is a sweeping claim: God is master even of deception. The Bible elsewhere shows God using deception within his rule (1 Kings 22:19–23; Ezekiel 14:9) and holds deceivers responsible (Deuteronomy 27:18). Jewish and Christian interpreters have read the line as saying that nothing escapes God's sovereignty, not that God approves of deceit (Aquinas). Critical scholars note that Job is building a picture of power with no visible moral order.

a: He marches advisers off barefoot
p: Sholal, 'barefoot' or 'stripped', describes prisoners of war led off by a conqueror.
b: Sholal appears in Micah 1:8 for the prophet going "barefoot and naked" as a sign of captivity. Assyrian reliefs show captives led away barefoot and partly stripped, and Isaiah walked barefoot as a sign that Egyptians would be led off that way (Isaiah 20:2–4). Counselors, judges, kings, priests and old families (12:17–19) are the leadership of a city; Job pictures God doing to them what a conqueror does.

a: He breaks the grip of kings
p: Literally 'he loosens the discipline of kings'. Most read 'bond' and see kings made captives.
b: Musar melakhim pitteach is "he loosens the discipline of kings." With a change of vowels (moser, "bond, fetter"), it becomes "he loosens the bonds of kings," which can mean he frees those kings have bound, or he undoes the belt that is a sign of royal authority. The second line, he ties an ezor (a plain waistcloth) around them, suggests kings reduced to captives or slaves. The Greek turns the verse the other way: "he seats kings on thrones and binds a belt on their waists." The Plain follows the common modern reading.

a: He pours scorn on the nobles
p: This line and the end of 12:24 appear together in Psalm 107:40.
b: Psalm 107:40 reads, in fresh wording, "pouring scorn on nobles, he made them wander in an empty waste with no road," which joins Job 12:21a and 12:24b word for word. Scholars debate who borrowed from whom. Some think the psalm quotes Job; others think both draw on a familiar hymn line. In the psalm the line is praise for God's care of the needy (Psalm 107:41); in Job it is part of a picture of God unmaking the world's order.

a: He lays bare things hidden deep in the dark
p: God brings deep things out of darkness. Daniel 2:22 praises God in very similar words.
b: Daniel, praising God for revealing Nebuchadnezzar's dream, says that God "uncovers deep things and hidden things. He knows what is in the dark" (Daniel 2:22). In Daniel this is God revealing mysteries to his servants. In Job's hymn it may mean God exposes the secret schemes of rulers, or drags the deep darkness of death itself into view (compare 26:6; 38:17). "Deep shadow" here is tsalmavet (see the note on 10:21).

a: sends them wandering in an empty waste with no road
p: Tohu is the 'formless' of Genesis 1:2. Leaders lose their sense and wander in a world unmade.
b: Tohu is the word for the formless earth before creation (Genesis 1:2) and for trackless desert (Deuteronomy 32:10). Rulers whom God strips of "heart" (sense) wander in a world with no roads, as if creation itself had come undone. The line is quoted in Psalm 107:40 (see the note on 12:21). In the next verse they grope like the blind and stagger like drunks, the curse of Deuteronomy 28:28–29.
r: Genesis 1:2; Deuteronomy 32:10; Deuteronomy 28:28–29; Psalm 107:40; Isaiah 24:20; Isaiah 59:10

a: I want to argue it out with God
p: Job wants to 'argue' (hokheach) with God, the verb behind the umpire (mokhiach) of 9:33.
b: Vehokheach el-El echpats, "and to argue with God I desire." The verb yakach runs through these chapters: the umpire (mokhiach) Job lacked (9:33), his "charge" (tokhachti, 13:6), God's rebuke of the friends (hokheach yokhiach, 13:10), and Job's resolve to "argue" his ways to God's face (okhiach, 13:15). Having no umpire, Job decides to argue his own case.

a: you are plasterers of lies
p: Two insults: the friends smear lies over the truth like plaster, and they are 'healers of nothing'.
b: Tofelei-sheqer are "smearers of falsehood," people who plaster over a crack (Psalm 119:69 uses the same verb for the arrogant who "smear me with lies"). Ezekiel uses a related picture for false prophets who whitewash a cracked wall (Ezekiel 13:10–15). Rof'ei elil are "healers of worthlessness": they came as comforters and doctors (2:11) but bring no cure. Elil is also the word for idols, "worthless gods," a sharp hint that their theology is a kind of idol. Jeremiah asked, "Is there no balm in Gilead?" (Jeremiah 8:22).

a: For you, silence would count as wisdom
p: Even a fool who keeps quiet is counted wise (Proverbs 17:28). The friends were wisest in their first week.
b: When the friends first came, they sat with Job seven days and nights and "Not one of them said anything to him" (2:13). Many readers think that was their best moment. Job now begs them to return to it. Proverbs 17:28 makes the same point with a smile: "Even a stubborn fool, if he stays silent, is counted as wise." Paul's advice to "weep along with those who weep" (Romans 12:15) is often quoted in sermons on this verse.

a: Is it for God that you speak what is unjust?
p: Job accuses the friends of defending God with lies. God's verdict in 42:7 agrees with him.
b: This is one of the boldest claims in the book: that a person can tell lies in defense of God, and that God does not want such defenders. The friends were speaking "for God" (la'el, "on God's behalf"); Job says they were favoring him like a corrupt witness who "lifts the face" of a powerful party (13:8; compare Leviticus 19:15). God's verdict at the end agrees: "You did not say what is right about me, the way my servant Job did" (42:7). Interpreters through the centuries (Calvin preached on this passage at length) have drawn the lesson that defending God with falsehood dishonors him.

a: Will you take his side because of who he is?
p: The idiom is 'lift his face': show favor to a party because of rank. Judges were forbidden to do it.
b: Panav tissa'un, "will you lift his face?" is the idiom for partiality in court: taking a person's side because of who they are rather than the facts (Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 10:17, where God "does not lift faces"). Job's charge is that the friends are acting like bribed witnesses for the most powerful party. In 13:10 he warns that God himself will rebuke them for it, a warning God fulfills in 42:7–8.
orig: הֲפָנָיו תִּשָּׂאוּן (hafanav tissa'un), 'will you lift his face?'

a: proverbs made of ash
p: The friends' 'memorable sayings' are proverbs of ash, and their defenses are made of clay.
b: Zikhronekhem, "your memorials," are the sayings the friends keep reciting from tradition (8:8). They are mishlei-efer, proverbs of ash, as useless as the ash heap Job sits on (2:8). Gabbim are mounds or the raised centers of shields; their defenses are clay, which breaks at a blow. "Dust and ashes" will come back in Job's last words (42:6).

a: hold my life in my open palm
p: To take one's life in one's hand means to risk it (Judges 12:3; 1 Samuel 19:5). Job knows his challenge may kill him.
b: "I put my life in my hand" is a Hebrew idiom for taking a deadly risk (Judges 12:3; 1 Samuel 19:5; 1 Samuel 28:21; Psalm 119:109). "Flesh in my teeth" is found only here; it may picture an animal carrying its prey, or a man holding on to his life at all costs. Job knows that approaching God may cost him his life (13:15), but he will do it anyway.

a: But I will argue for the way I have lived, right to his face
p: Both readings end the same way: Job will argue to God's face. Is that faith or defiance?
b: Akh-derakhai el-panav okhiach, "yet my ways to his face I will argue." On the two readings of the first line, "I have nothing left to hope for" (written text) or "I will hope in him" (reading tradition), see the variant, which sets out the witnesses and the arguments. Both readings end here. On the reading tradition, faith and argument stand together: Job hopes in God even as he argues with him, as in the lament psalms and Abraham's plea (Genesis 18:25); the Mishnah uses the verse to show Job served God "out of love" (Sotah 5:5), and Christian preaching has made the KJV line a motto of trust. On the written text, Job expects death and argues anyway, because his integrity matters more than his life (27:5–6). Many readers find that just as much an act of faith: Job still believes God is the one to whom a case can be made.

a: Even this will turn into my rescue
p: Paul quotes the Greek of this line word for word in Philippians 1:19, writing from prison.
b: The Greek of 13:16a, touto moi apobēsetai eis sōtērian, "this will turn out for my deliverance," appears word for word in Philippians 1:19, where Paul, in prison and facing possible death, writes, "I know that this will turn out for my rescue." Many scholars think Paul is echoing Job on purpose: like Job, he is a righteous sufferer who trusts that God will vindicate him in the end, whether by life or by death (Philippians 1:20). In Job the "this" is his very boldness: only an innocent man would dare to come before God.

a: I have set my case in order
p: 'Arakh mishpat is to set out a legal case in order, like an army in battle lines. Job is ready for trial.
b: 'Arakhti mishpat means "I have arranged a case": the verb is used for drawing up troops in order (1 Samuel 17:8) and for laying out words in argument (32:14; 33:5). Job has prepared his defense and is confident: "I know that I am the one who is right" (ani etsdaq), the legal verb of 9:2. He will set out the case again in 23:4 and sign it in 31:35.

a: If someone could, I would hold my tongue and breathe my last
p: If anyone could prove a charge against him, Job would fall silent and die. Silence would mean admitting guilt.
b: In a lawsuit, silence means conceding (Isaiah 53:7 is famous for a servant who does not open his mouth). Job means that if anyone could really bring a valid case against him, he would accept it and die. Some read the line the other way: "if I kept silent now, I would die," meaning he must speak or burst (32:19–20, where Elihu says something like this). The Hebrew ki-'attah allows both.

a: Just two things, do not do them to me
p: Job turns to God and names two conditions: stop the pain, and stop the terror. Then he can speak.
b: From 13:20 Job speaks to God directly until the end of chapter 14. His two conditions (13:21) repeat 9:34. Job is not asking for his suffering to be explained, but for the basic conditions of a fair trial: that the defendant not be tortured or terrified while he speaks. Then either God may call and Job answer, or Job speak and God reply (13:22). God will eventually do just this, in reverse order: he speaks from the storm, asks his questions, and Job answers (38:1–3; 40:1–5; 42:1–6).

a: Why do you treat me as your enemy?
p: In Hebrew 'enemy' (oyev) sounds almost like Job's name (Iyyov). The rabbis noticed the wordplay.
b: Le'oyev lakh, "as an enemy to you." Job's name, Iyyov, and oyev, "enemy," differ by one letter. The Talmud imagines Job asking whether God had confused Iyyov with oyev (Bava Batra 16a; see the note on 9:17). Some scholars think the name was chosen for this sound. The hidden face is the lament psalms' image of feeling abandoned by God (Psalm 13:1; Psalm 88:14). Job will say again that God counts him an enemy (19:11; 33:10).

a: you hand me the guilt of my young days as my inheritance
p: Job wonders whether the faults of his youth are being charged against him now.
b: Job does not claim to be sinless. He allows for the ordinary faults of youth, which he thinks God has written down as "bitter charges" (merorot) and is now making him "inherit." The psalmist prays for those sins to be forgotten (Psalm 25:7). Job's complaint is that God, unlike the God of the psalm, seems to keep the old record open. Zophar had said God forgets part of Job's guilt (11:6); Job feels the opposite.

a: you scratch a mark on the bottoms of my feet
p: Wooden stocks for the feet, and a mark like a slave's brand or a line the prisoner may not cross.
b: Sad is a wooden block with holes for a prisoner's feet (33:11; compare Acts 16:24). Al-shorshei raglai titchaqqeh is literally "on the roots of my feet you carve (a mark)." It may mean God brands the soles of Job's feet like a slave or prisoner so he can be tracked, or draws a line around them that he must not cross (compare 14:5). Elihu quotes the first two lines in 33:11, "He clamps my feet in the stocks; / he keeps an eye on every path I take," as an example of Job's complaint.

a: And he wears out like rot
p: 'He' has no clear subject. Many scholars move this verse after 14:2, where it fits the frailty of 'man'.
b: The verse speaks of "he" wasting away like rot or a moth-eaten garment, but the verses around it speak of "me" and "you." Some read "he" as Job speaking of himself in the third person, which happens in laments. Many modern scholars and some translations (NEB, REB) move 13:28 after 14:2, where "he" means the mortal of 14:1. Others think it is a deliberate bridge from Job's own case to the human condition in chapter 14. No ancient witness has the verse in a different place; the Greek reads it here. The moth is a common picture for slow decay (Isaiah 50:9; Isaiah 51:8; Matthew 6:19–20).

a: A human, born of a woman
p: 'Born of a woman' stresses human weakness. The phrase is used in burial services and in the New Testament.
b: Adam yelud ishah, "a human born of a woman," names a person by weakness and mortality. Eliphaz and Bildad use it to say no human can be pure before God (15:14; 25:4). Jesus uses it of all humanity (Matthew 11:11), and Paul says God's Son was "born of a woman" (Galatians 4:4), sharing that frailty. The English burial service of the Book of Common Prayer (1549 and later) opens its words at the grave with a paraphrase of 14:1–2, so this passage has been read over countless Christian graves.

a: has his fill of turmoil
p: Rogez is agitation, turmoil, rage. It is the word Job used for his own condition in 3:17 and 3:26.
b: Seva'-rogez means "sated with turmoil." Rogez is the restless trembling and agitation of 3:17 ("there the wicked stop their raging") and 3:26 ("turmoil comes"). Life is "short of days" but long on trouble, a sad reversal of the patriarchs who died "full of days" (Genesis 35:29; 42:17).

a: Like a blossom he comes out, and then he droops
p: The fading flower and the passing shadow are favorite images for human life across the Bible.
b: "Like a flower" (tsits) and "like a shadow" (tsel) are the stock pictures of a short life (8:9; Psalm 103:15–16; Psalm 144:4). Isaiah turns the flower into a contrast with God's lasting word: "the grass dries up, the flower wilts, but our God's word will stand forever" (Isaiah 40:6–8), which James and 1 Peter take up (James 1:10–11; 1 Peter 1:24–25). Job has no such contrast yet; for him the shadow simply "does not stay."

a: Who can make what is clean come out of what is unclean?
p: Many Christians, after Augustine, read this as a text on inherited sin; others see human frailty.
b: The Hebrew may be read as a question ("Who can bring clean from unclean? No one") or as a wish ("If only someone could bring clean from unclean!"; mi yitten usually means "if only"). Job's point in context is that a frail, impure human cannot meet God's standard, so God should go easy on him (14:5–6). The Greek of 14:4–5 reads: "Who will be clean from filth? No one, even if his life on earth is one day," and the Latin Vulgate has "who can make clean one conceived of unclean seed?" Through these versions the verse became a classic text on original sin for Augustine (Confessions 1.7) and later Christian theology (compare Psalm 51:5). Jewish readers, and many Christian commentators today, see in it human weakness and ritual impurity, not inherited guilt. See the "Where Christians differ" card for chapter 14.
orig: מִי־יִתֵּן טָהוֹר מִטָּמֵא לֹא אֶחָד (mi-yitten tahor mittame' lo echad)

a: if you have set him bounds he will not cross
p: Chuqqo, 'his limit' or 'his limits' (Ketiv and Qere differ by one letter), is God's fixed term for a life.
b: Charutsim, "cut, decided," describes days measured out in advance, and choq is a fixed limit, the word used of the bounds God set for the sea (38:10; Proverbs 8:29; Jeremiah 5:22). The written text has the singular "his limit," the reading tradition the plural "his limits"; the meaning is the same. Psalm 39:4–5 and 139:16 also speak of days numbered by God.

a: so that like a hired man he can be content with his day
p: Job asks God to look away and let a man finish his day like a laborer, glad just to rest at sunset.
b: Ad-yirtseh kesakhir yomo is "until he is content with (or pays off) his day like a hired man." Job used the hired worker in 7:1–2: a man who longs for evening and his wages. Here he asks that God stop watching (she'eh, "look away," as in 7:19, "Will you not look away from me?") so that a human can at least enjoy the end of his working day. Some read yirtseh as "complete, pay off," as in Leviticus 26:34.

a: A tree, at least, has hope
p: A cut tree sprouts again from its stump. Job sees no such hope for a human.
b: Many trees in the Levant, such as olives, sycamores and terebinths, send up new shoots from a cut stump. The prophets used this picture: "From Jesse's stump a shoot will come out" (Isaiah 11:1), "Its stump is a holy seed" (Isaiah 6:13), and Nebuchadnezzar's stump is left in the ground (Daniel 4:15). Job uses it to say the opposite of humans: a tree has hope, a man does not. The verb "come back with new growth" (yachalif) shares a root with the "relief" Job longs for in 14:14 (chalifati). Later in the book Job says God "rips my hope up by the roots like a tree" (19:10).
orig: כִּי יֵשׁ לָעֵץ תִּקְוָה (ki yesh la'ets tiqvah)

a: and where is he then?
p: Ve'ayyo, 'and where is he?', is one word in Hebrew. It echoes Job's last line in chapter 7.
b: Ve'ayyo, "and where is he?" is a single short word, a question with no answer. It echoes 7:21 ("I will not be there") and 7:8–10 ("his place will not know him any more"). The verbs of the verse are frank: yamut "he dies," yechelash "he grows weak," yigva' "he breathes his last." Gever is a man in his strength: even the strong end this way.

a: Water runs out of the sea
p: 14:11 is almost word for word Isaiah 19:5, where the Nile dries up in judgment on Egypt.
b: Isaiah 19:5 says, in nearly the same Hebrew, "the waters will dry up from the sea, and the river will be parched and dry," of the Nile failing. One text may borrow from the other, or both from a common phrase. Here the picture is of a lake or the Nile in drought, a body of water that simply disappears. Unlike the tree, it does not come back.
