The Hebrew yam may mean the sea or a large lake or river.

a: Until the heavens are gone, they do not wake up
t: Sleep until the heavens are gone
p: To Job this means 'never'. Later readers heard a hint of resurrection at the end of the heavens.
b: 'Ad-bilti shamayim, "until there are no heavens," is for Job a way of saying "never," since the heavens last forever (Psalm 89:29; Jeremiah 31:35–36). The image of death as sleep (Psalm 13:3; Daniel 12:2) carries its own hope: sleepers can wake. Later readers, who believed the heavens would one day pass away and the dead would rise (Isaiah 26:19; Isaiah 65:17; Daniel 12:2; Revelation 20:11–13), read Job's words as unknowingly pointing to that day. The Greek has "until the heaven is unstitched." Some Christian traditions also read the verse on whether the dead are conscious before the resurrection; see the "Where Christians differ" card for this chapter.
r: 3:13; 7:21; Psalm 13:3; Psalm 89:29; Isaiah 26:19; Isaiah 51:6; Daniel 12:2; Revelation 20:11–13; 2 Peter 3:10

a: I wish you would tuck me away in Sheol
p: Job's daring wish: that Sheol could be a hiding place until God's anger passes, and then God would remember him.
b: For the first time Job imagines Sheol, the realm of the dead, not as the end but as a shelter. God would hide him there like a treasure (tatspineni, the verb for storing valuables), set a time (choq, as in 14:5), and "remember" him, as God remembered Noah in the ark (Genesis 8:1). Isaiah 26:20 uses a similar picture: "hide for just a moment until the fury goes past." Job knows no one comes back from Sheol (7:9), so this is a wish, not a belief. But it is the first step toward the bolder hopes of 16:19 and 19:25–27.
orig: מִי יִתֵּן בִּשְׁאוֹל תַּצְפִּנֵנִי (mi yitten bish'ol tatspineni)

a: When a man dies, can he come back to life?
t: If a man dies, will he live?
p: Job seems to expect 'no'. The Greek turns his question into a statement: he will live.
b: Im-yamut gever hayichyeh, "if a man dies, will he live?" In context the expected answer is no (14:10–12). Yet Job goes on to describe what he would do if the answer were yes: wait through his hard service until his "relief" came, answer when God called (14:15). The Greek turns the question into a statement: "For if a person dies, he will live, when he has completed the days of his life; I will wait until I come to be again." It has no question word, so the natural reading is an affirmation of life after death (Brenton's 1844 English prints a question mark). The Greek translator seems to have read Job's doubtful question as a hope, as the Greek Job does again in its added ending at 42:17 ("It is written that he will rise again with those the Lord raises up"). See the variant. The Vulgate's "until my change comes" (immutatio mea) led Christian readers to Paul: "all of us will be changed" (1 Corinthians 15:51). Jewish readers took the verse as a question that the book's later chapters, and the rabbis' belief in the resurrection, would answer.

a: Through every day of my hard duty I would wait
p: Tsava is military service; chalifah is the relief, the next shift coming to take over the watch.
b: Kol-yemei tseva'i is "all the days of my service," the word for an army tour of duty, used in 7:1 ("a soldier's tour of duty"). Chalifati is "my relief, my replacement," the fresh guard who comes to end a soldier's watch (compare chalifot, 10:17). Job pictures life, and maybe death too, as a long watch; he would wait patiently if he knew relief would come. The KJV's "till my change come" follows the Latin.

a: you would yearn for the thing your hands had made
p: Job imagines God missing him, longing for his own handiwork. It reverses 10:3, where God rejects what his hands made.
b: Lema'aseh yadekha tikhsof, "for the work of your hands you will long." The verb kasaf is strong longing, as for home (Genesis 31:30; Psalm 84:2). In 10:3 Job asked why God would reject the work of his hands; here he imagines God longing for it. It is one of the most hopeful lines in Job's speeches: the God who made him would one day want him back. Then God would call and Job answer, the very conversation Job asked for in 13:22.

a: Then you would count each step I take
p: The Hebrew says 'for now'. It may continue Job's hope or return to his present complaint.
b: Ki-'attah tse'aday tispor, "for now you count my steps." If 14:16–17 continues the wish of 14:13–15, "now" means "then, in that time": God would watch Job's steps with care and not keep watch for his sins. If it returns to the present, Job says God counts every step he takes in order to catch him (as in 13:27; 31:4). The second line can also be read as a question, "do you not watch over my sin?" (KJV). The Plain follows the first reading, which fits 14:17.

a: You would tie up my rebellion in a pouch with a seal on it
p: A sealed bag could mean sins kept as evidence, or sins put away out of sight. The plaster recalls 13:4.
b: A sealed pouch (tseror) held valuables or documents (Genesis 42:35; 1 Samuel 25:29). Hosea uses the picture for guilt stored up for judgment: "Ephraim's guilt is wrapped up in a bundle; his sin is locked away in storage" (Hosea 13:12). But in the hopeful setting of 14:13–16, the seal more likely means the sins are put away for good, and "plaster over" (tafal) means God would cover Job's guilt, the same verb Job used for the friends who "plaster" lies (13:4). Micah has a similar hope: God will throw all their sins into the depths of the sea (Micah 7:19).

a: that is how you wipe out a human's hope
p: The hope of 14:13–17 collapses. Even mountains and stones wear away; so God wears away human hope.
b: The wish of 14:13–17 gives way to the hard facts of nature: mountains fall, cliffs shift, water grinds stones and floods wash away soil. If even these erode, a human has no chance. The word "hope" (tiqvah) closes the circle begun with the tree that "has hope" (14:7). The chapter, and the first round of the debate, ends in darkness. Many readers see the pattern of Job's speeches here: hope rises, then falls, then rises higher the next time (16:19; 19:25).

a: you alter his face and send him away
p: Death changes a person's face. 'Send him away' is the verb used for sending someone off for good.
b: Meshanneh fanav, "changing his face," is the change death brings to the body, or the face of a person aged and worn by grief. Vatteshallechehu, "and you sent him away," is the verb for dismissing a servant or divorcing a wife (Deuteronomy 24:1). God "prevails" (titqefehu) over the human for good (lanetsach), and he is gone.

a: If his sons rise to honor, he never knows
p: In Sheol a father does not know how his children fare. Job, whose children died, speaks from grief.
b: The Hebrew Bible usually pictures the dead as cut off from the world of the living: "the dead know nothing" (Ecclesiastes 9:5–6; compare Isaiah 63:16; Psalm 88:10–12). For an ancient father, seeing his sons honored was the crown of life (42:16). Job, whose sons and daughters are dead, imagines himself dead and not even knowing what becomes of his family. Later Jewish and Christian beliefs about the dead knowing and praying for the living (2 Maccabees 15:12–14, Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians; Luke 16:27–28; Hebrews 12:1) are not in view here.

a: All he has is the ache of his own flesh
p: The dead, or the dying, feel only their own pain and grief.
b: The Hebrew says "only his flesh upon him aches, and his soul upon him mourns." Many read this as a picture of the dead in Sheol, who still feel the decay of the body and a dim grief, as some ancient Near Eastern texts imagined. Others think it describes the dying man, wrapped up in his own pain. Either way it ends Job's speech, and the first cycle of the debate, with a human being alone with his suffering. Eliphaz will open the second round in 15:2.
